title: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
summary: Vectors, dot products and matrices as maps, then rank, inverses, projections and least squares, eigenvectors and the SVD, tensor shapes and broadcasting, and how they power linear layers and attention.
outcomes: Explain a vector as both a list of numbers and an arrow, and compute sums, scalings, norms and distances
Compute a dot product and cosine similarity and explain why raw dot products mix direction with length
Explain a matrix-vector product in both the row view and the column view
Predict the shape and cost of a matrix product and explain why AB usually differs from BA
Use span, rank and the determinant to decide if Ax = b is solvable, and solve it without forming the inverse
Project onto a line or column space and fit least squares with the normal equations
Compute eigenvectors and the SVD of a 2 x 2 matrix and use them for power iteration, low-rank approximation and PCA
Predict tensor shapes under batched matmul and broadcasting, and read y = xW^T + b and attention scores as dot products

lessons.title: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time

blocks.md: Almost everything a neural network touches is stored as a list of numbers: a pixel patch, a user profile, a word's embedding (a learned list of numbers that stands for the word). Linear algebra is the toolkit for doing arithmetic on such lists all at once. This course builds the ideas you need to read ML papers and code: vectors, the dot product and matrices first, then what a matrix can reach and undo (rank and inverses), projections and least squares, eigenvectors and the SVD, and the tensor shapes real code uses.

A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers, called its **components**. The vector $\mathbf{a} = [3, 4]$ has 2 components, so it lives in 2-dimensional space, written $\mathbb{R}^2$. The R in that name stands for the real numbers, every point on the number line including negatives and fractions, and the exponent says how many of them make one vector: $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the set of all pairs. An embedding with 768 components lives in $\mathbb{R}^{768}$. The number of components is the vector's **dimension**.

The same vector has a second reading: an arrow from the origin (the point $(0, 0)$ where the axes cross) to the point $(3, 4)$, going 3 steps along the first axis and 4 along the second. Programmers use the list view; geometry uses the arrow view. The power of linear algebra is that every operation makes sense in both views, so you can compute with lists and reason with arrows.

Two operations are at the heart of every vector space:

- **Addition** works component by component: $[3,4] + [1,2] = [4,6]$. As arrows, you place $\mathbf{b}$ at the tip of $\mathbf{a}$ and the sum points to where you end up.
- **Scalar multiplication** multiplies every component by one number (a **scalar**): $2[3,4] = [6,8]$. As an arrow, it stretches by 2 without turning. A negative scalar flips the arrow to point the opposite way.

blocks.title: Component-wise arithmetic on a = [3, 4] and b = [1, 2]

scenes.caption: Two vectors in R^2. Index 0 is the first component, index 1 the second. Operations line up components with the same index.
a + b: add index 0 (3 + 1 = 4) and index 1 (4 + 2 = 6). As arrows, walking along a and then along b ends at (4, 6).
2a: every component doubles to [6, 8]. Same direction as a, twice as long.
a - b = a + (-1)b = [2, 2]. Subtraction gives the arrow that goes from the tip of b to the tip of a.
Length of a: sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5. The result row now holds the squares 9 and 16 that get summed.

blocks.md: The **length** (or **norm**) of a vector is the Pythagorean distance from the origin to its tip. Here is where it comes from: the arrow to $(3, 4)$ is the long side (the hypotenuse) of a right triangle whose legs are 3 along the first axis and 4 along the second. Pythagoras says the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squared legs: $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$, so the length is $\sqrt{25} = 5$. For $\mathbf{b} = [1,2]$ it is $\sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$. In 3 dimensions you apply the same step twice: first the diagonal across the floor, then the hypotenuse up to the tip, which adds a third square. Repeating that gives the rule for any dimension: square every component, add, take the square root.

blocks.caption: The Euclidean (L2) norm: the straight-line length of ordinary geometry, called L2 because it raises each component to the power 2. A unit vector has norm 1; dividing any nonzero vector by its norm gives the unit vector pointing the same way.

blocks.reveal: **Almost, but no.** $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} = [4,6]$ and $\sqrt{16+36} = \sqrt{52} \approx 7.211$, slightly less than 7.236. Lengths add exactly only when the arrows point the same way. Otherwise the shortcut is shorter than the two legs: this is the **triangle inequality**, $\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\| \le \|\mathbf{a}\| + \|\mathbf{b}\|$. Here a and b point in nearly the same direction (about 10 degrees apart; the next lesson shows how to compute that angle), so the gap is small.

blocks.md:
The L2 norm is not the only way to measure size. Goodfellow et al. list the ones ML uses most:

- **L1 norm** (also called the Manhattan norm): add the absolute values, $|3| + |4| = 7$ for $\mathbf{a}$. It grows at the same rate everywhere, even right next to 0, so it is used when telling exactly-zero entries from small nonzero ones matters, as in L1 regularization.
- **Max norm** (L-infinity): the largest absolute component, 4 for $\mathbf{a}$.

The **distance** between two vectors is the norm of their difference. For $\mathbf{a} = [3,4]$ and $\mathbf{b} = [1,2]$, $\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b} = [2,2]$, so the L2 distance is $\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ and the L1 distance is 4. Matrices get a size too: the **Frobenius norm** squares every entry, adds them all and takes the square root, the L2 norm of the matrix read as one long list.

Adding vectors of different dimensions is undefined in math. NumPy and PyTorch will sometimes *broadcast* (silently repeat) a smaller array to fit, so shape bugs can produce a result instead of an error. Always know the shape of every array you add. The tensors lesson gives the exact rule.
A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

blocks.question: An embedding $\mathbf{v} = [0.6, 0.8]$ is multiplied by the scalar $-2$. What happens to it as an arrow?
options: It points the opposite way and its length becomes 2
It rotates 90 degrees and keeps its length
It points the opposite way and its length becomes -2
It keeps its direction and its length becomes 2
blocks.explain: $-2\mathbf{v} = [-1.2, -1.6]$, whose norm is $\sqrt{1.44+2.56} = 2$. The minus sign flips the direction; lengths are never negative, so the length is $|{-2}| \times 1 = 2$. Scaling never rotates by anything other than 0 or 180 degrees.

blocks.question: You store 1,000 user profiles, each with 32 numeric features, as vectors. Which statement is right?
options: Each profile is a vector in R^1000
You cannot add two profiles because their features have different meanings
Each profile is a vector in R^32, and you can add two profiles component by component
Each feature is a vector in R^32
blocks.explain: Each profile has 32 components, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^{32}$. The math allows adding any two vectors of the same dimension; whether the sum is *meaningful* depends on the features, but averaging profiles (add, then scale by 1/2) is a common and legal operation.

blocks.question: What is the L2 distance between $[1, 5]$ and $[4, 1]$, and what is the L1 distance?
options: L2 distance 7, L1 distance 5
L2 distance 25, L1 distance 7
L2 distance 5, L1 distance 7
L2 distance 5, L1 distance 5
blocks.explain: The difference is $[-3, 4]$. L2: $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$. L1: $|{-3}| + |4| = 7$. 25 is the squared L2 distance, before the square root. The L1 distance is never smaller than the L2 distance, because walking along the axes is never shorter than the straight line.

lessons.title: The dot product: one number that measures alignment

blocks.md: The **dot product** of two vectors with the same dimension multiplies matching components and adds the results. It turns two vectors into one scalar. For $\mathbf{a}=[3,4]$ and $\mathbf{b}=[1,2]$: $3 \times 1 + 4 \times 2 = 11$.

blocks.tex: \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \cdots + a_n b_n
blocks.caption: Algebraic definition. It is symmetric: a.b = b.a.

blocks.md: Why is this one number so useful? Because it also has a geometric meaning. If $\theta$ is the angle between the two arrows, the dot product equals the product of the lengths times $\cos\theta$. The cosine is 1 when the arrows point the same way, 0 when they are perpendicular, and -1 when they point in opposite directions.

blocks.caption: Geometric form. Both formulas give the same number; the course examples check this with real values.

blocks.md: Where does the cosine come from? Draw the triangle whose sides are $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and the arrow $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}$ joining their tips. The **law of cosines**, Pythagoras extended to any angle, says the squared length of that third side is the squared length of a plus the squared length of b, minus 2 times both lengths times $\cos\theta$; at 90 degrees the extra term is 0 and you get Pythagoras back. Now compute the same squared length from components: each component gives $(a_i - b_i)^2 = a_i^2 + b_i^2 - 2a_ib_i$, so the total is the squared length of a plus the squared length of b, minus 2 times the dot product. Both describe one number, so the dot product must equal the two lengths times $\cos\theta$. With our pair: $\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b} = [2, 2]$ has squared length 8, so $25 + 5 - 8 = 22$, and half of 22 is 11, exactly the dot product.

blocks.caption: The law of cosines (middle) and the component expansion (right) describe the same squared length, so the dot product must equal the two lengths times cos theta.

blocks.md: Now use it to find the angle. The two lengths multiply to $5 \times 2.236 = 11.18$, so $\cos\theta = 11/11.18 = 0.984$, and $\theta \approx 10.3$ degrees, the angle whose cosine is 0.984 (found with the inverse cosine, arccos): the arrows almost line up. Rotate $\mathbf{a}$ by 90 degrees to $[-4, 3]$ and the dot product with $\mathbf{a}$ is $-12 + 12 = 0$. Flip it to $-\mathbf{a}$ and you get $-25$.

blocks.title: Dot product as a function of the angle

scenes.caption: With |a||b| = 11.18 (our pair), the dot product is 11 at 10.3 degrees. It falls as the angle opens and crosses 0 at 90 degrees.
Two vectors of length 5, like a and a turned copy of a, have |a||b| = 25: the dot product runs from +25 (same direction) to -25 (opposite). At 0 degrees it is a . a = |a|^2 = 25.
Short vectors (|a||b| = 2) give small dot products at every angle. The sign tells you the direction; the size mixes direction with length.

blocks.md: A second geometric reading: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} / \|\mathbf{a}\|$ is the **projection** length, how far $\mathbf{b}$ reaches along the direction of $\mathbf{a}$. To see why, drop a perpendicular from the tip of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the line through $\mathbf{a}$: it makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the length of b, so the side along $\mathbf{a}$ is the length of b times $\cos\theta$, which by the geometric form is the dot product divided by the length of a. For our pair it is $11/5 = 2.2$. If you think of $\mathbf{a}$ as a unit-length detector of some pattern, the dot product reports how much of that pattern $\mathbf{b}$ contains.

Now a toy embedding example (made-up 4-dimensional vectors; real embeddings are learned and have hundreds of components). Query: *cat* $=[0.8, 0.6, 0.1, 0]$. Candidates: *kitten* $=[0.4, 0.3, 0.05, 0]$, which is exactly half of cat, *dog* $=[0.6, 0.7, 0.2, 0.1]$ and *car* $=[0.1, 0, 0.9, 0.7]$.

blocks.title: Computing cat . dog one component at a time

scenes.caption: Line up components with the same index. Nothing computed yet.
Index 0: 0.8 x 0.6 = 0.48. Both vectors are large here, so this pair contributes most.
Index 1: 0.6 x 0.7 = 0.42, running sum 0.90.
Index 2: 0.1 x 0.2 = 0.02. Index 3: 0 x 0.1 = 0, because cat has nothing in that component.

blocks.prompt: Rank kitten, dog and car by their **dot product** with cat. Does the winner match your intuition that kitten is the closest word?
blocks.reveal: Dot products: dog **0.92**, kitten **0.505**, car **0.17**. Dog wins, even though kitten points in *exactly* the same direction as cat. Kitten loses only because it is a shorter vector (norm 0.50 versus 0.95 for dog). The raw dot product mixes *direction* with *length*.

blocks.md: The fix is to divide out the lengths. **Cosine similarity** is the dot product of the two vectors after scaling each to unit length, which is exactly $\cos\theta$. It ignores length and keeps only direction, so it always lies between -1 and 1.

blocks.title: Similarity to cat: raw dot product versus cosine

scenes.caption: Raw dot product with cat. Dog (0.92) beats kitten (0.505) because dog's vector is longer.
Cosine similarity: kitten 1.000 (same direction), dog 0.965, car 0.148. Dividing out the lengths restores the intuitive ranking.

blocks.md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

Many vector databases (stores that hold embeddings and return the ones nearest a query) and embedding pipelines normalize every vector to unit length once, at write time. After that, the cheap dot product *is* the cosine similarity, because both norms are 1.

$\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

blocks.question: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the angle between them?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
45 degrees
It depends on their dimension
blocks.explain: For unit vectors the dot product equals $\cos\theta$, and the cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5. The formula holds in any dimension, because any two vectors lie in one flat plane (the plane of all their combinations), and the angle is measured inside it.

blocks.question: A search system ranks documents by raw dot product with the query embedding. Users complain that long, rambling documents always win. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Use more embedding dimensions
Square every dot product before ranking
Add a constant to every component of the query
Rank by cosine similarity, or normalize all embeddings to unit length
blocks.explain: If document vectors grow longer with document length, the dot product rewards that length. Dividing by the norms (cosine) keeps only direction. More dimensions or squaring the score keeps the length effect; adding a constant changes the query's direction, not the bias.

lessons.title: A matrix is a function that moves every vector

blocks.md: A **matrix** is a rectangular grid of numbers with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, called an $m \times n$ matrix. Its most important job: multiplying it by a vector with $n$ components produces a new vector with $m$ components. So a matrix *is* a function from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$, and a special kind, a **linear map**: it sends sums to sums and scaled vectors to scaled vectors.

There are two equivalent ways to compute $A\mathbf{x}$, and you should know both.

1. **Row view:** output component $i$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with $\mathbf{x}$.
2. **Column view:** the output is a weighted sum of the columns of $A$, with weights $x_1, x_2, \ldots$

blocks.caption: Row view (middle) and column view (right) give the same answer.

blocks.title: Row view then column view of A x with x = [1, 2]

scenes.caption: A is 2 x 2. It will act on x = [1, 2].
Row view, output 1: row 1 dot x = 2 x 1 + 1 x 2 = 4.
Row view, output 2: row 2 dot x = 1 x 1 + 3 x 2 = 7. Output: [4, 7].
Column view: take 1 copy of column 1, [2, 1] ...
... plus 2 copies of column 2, [1, 3]: [2, 1] + [2, 6] = [4, 7]. Same answer, different story.

blocks.md: The column view gives the key geometric fact. Feed in the **basis vectors** $\mathbf{e}_1 = [1,0]$ and $\mathbf{e}_2 = [0,1]$ (unit arrows along each axis). They are called a **basis** because every vector in the plane is built from them in exactly one way (the span and rank lesson says precisely what that takes). $A\mathbf{e}_1$ picks out column 1 and $A\mathbf{e}_2$ picks out column 2. Every other vector is a combination $x_1\mathbf{e}_1 + x_2\mathbf{e}_2$, and linearity means it lands on $x_1(\text{col }1) + x_2(\text{col }2)$. **The columns tell you where the axes land, and that determines where everything lands.**

blocks.title: Three matrices acting on x = [3, 4]

scenes.caption: Rotation by 90 degrees counterclockwise: columns [0, 1] and [-1, 0] are where e1 and e2 land. [3, 4] goes to [-4, 3]. Length stays 5, and x . Ax = 0.
Scaling diag(2, 0.5), the matrix with 2 and 0.5 on its diagonal and 0 elsewhere: stretch axis 1 by 2, squash axis 2 by half. [3, 4] goes to [6, 2]. Different stretch per axis changes direction too.
Shear [[1, 1], [0, 1]]: e1 stays, e2 tilts to [1, 1]. [3, 4] goes to [3 + 4, 4] = [7, 4]. Grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced.

blocks.md: In code, the row view is a double loop: for each output component, accumulate a dot product. An $m \times n$ matrix times a vector costs $m \times n$ multiply-adds. Step through it below with the same $A$ and $\mathbf{x}$.

blocks.title: Matrix-vector product as a double loop
blocks.code:
A = [[2, 1],
     [1, 3]]
x = [1, 2]
y = [0, 0]
for i in range(2):          # each output row
    for j in range(2):      # dot product of row i with x
        y[i] += A[i][j] * x[j]
print(y)

scenes.caption: Set up A (2 x 2), the input x and an output y of zeros, one slot per row of A.
i = 0, j = 1: y[0] += 1 x 2. Row 1 dot x is finished: 4.
i = 1, j = 1: y[1] += 3 x 2. Four multiply-adds for a 2 x 2 matrix.
Result matches the column view: [4, 7].

blocks.prompt: A matrix $B$ sends $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $[2, 0]$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ to $[0, 3]$. Without writing $B$, where does $[1, 1]$ go?
blocks.reveal: $[1,1] = \mathbf{e}_1 + \mathbf{e}_2$, so it lands on $[2,0] + [0,3] = [2, 3]$. That is all linearity means: knowing where the basis vectors go determines the whole map. Here $B = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, its columns are those two images.

blocks.md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU, explained next) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

An **activation function** is a fixed function applied to every component after a layer's affine step. The most common is ReLU, short for rectified linear unit, which outputs the larger of 0 and its input, written $\max(0, x)$: positive values pass through and negatives become zero. Its graph is a line bent at 0, and that bend breaks linearity: ReLU of -1 plus ReLU of 1 is 1, but ReLU of their sum, 0, is zero. Without such a bend, depth would buy nothing: applying one affine map after another is again a single affine map, one matrix plus one bias, as the next lesson's rule for composing matrices shows.
$A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

blocks.question: $A$ has shape $3 \times 5$. Which input can it multiply, and what comes out?
options: A vector with 5 components; out comes a vector with 3
A vector with 3 components; out comes a vector with 5
Any vector; out comes a 3 x 5 matrix
A vector with 15 components; out comes a scalar
blocks.explain: Each row has 5 entries and is dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so $\mathbf{x}$ needs 5 components. There are 3 rows, so 3 output components. An $m \times n$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$.

blocks.question: Is $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ guaranteed to satisfy $f(2\mathbf{x}) = 2f(\mathbf{x})$ for every matrix $A$?
options: Only if A is square
Only if A is a rotation
Yes, for every matrix A
No, only if A has no negative entries
blocks.explain: Each output component is $\sum_j A_{ij}(2x_j) = 2\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$. Scaling passes through any matrix. This is half of the definition of linearity; the other half is $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + f(\mathbf{y})$.

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes

blocks.md: If a matrix is a function, multiplying two matrices is **composing** two functions. $(AB)\mathbf{x}$ means: first apply $B$, then apply $A$. The product $AB$ is a single matrix that does both in one step. That is why the rule for computing it looks the way it does. Derive it from the matrix-vector lesson: column $j$ of $AB$ is where $AB$ sends the basis vector $\mathbf{e}_j$. $B$ sends $\mathbf{e}_j$ to its own column $j$, and $A$ then moves that column, so column $j$ of $AB$ is $A$ times column $j$ of $B$. By the row view, entry $i$ of that result is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$.

blocks.caption: Entry (i, j) is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.

blocks.md: Shapes must chain. If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, the inner sizes match ($n$) and $C$ is $m \times p$. If the inner sizes differ, the product is undefined, and NumPy's `@` raises an error. Computing $C$ takes $m \times n \times p$ multiply-adds: $mp$ entries, each a dot product of length $n$.

Worked example. $M = \begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix}$ is $2 \times 3$ and $N = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\\0&4\end{bmatrix}$ is $3 \times 2$. The inner sizes are both 3, so $MN$ is $2 \times 2$.

blocks.title: Filling C = MN one dot product at a time

scenes.caption: C will be 2 x 2: one entry per (row of M, column of N) pair. All entries start at 0 as placeholders.

blocks.prompt: $M$ is $2 \times 3$ and $N$ is $3 \times 2$. Is $NM$ the same as $MN$?
blocks.reveal: **Not even the same shape.** $NM$ is $3 \times 3$: $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\2&5&3\\0&4&12\end{bmatrix}$, while $MN$ is $2 \times 2$. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: order matters, just like putting on socks then shoes is different from shoes then socks.

blocks.md: Even square matrices usually do not commute. Take the rotation $R$ by 90 degrees and the scaling $S = \text{diag}(2, 0.5)$ from the last lesson and apply both to $\mathbf{x} = [3,4]$. Rotate then scale ($SR\mathbf{x}$) gives $[-8, 1.5]$. Scale then rotate ($RS\mathbf{x}$) gives $[-2, 6]$.

blocks.title: Order matters: S R x versus R S x for x = [3, 4]

scenes.caption: Both paths start at x = [3, 4].
Path 1 rotates first: R x = [-4, 3]. Path 2 scales first: S x = [6, 2].
Path 1 now scales: S [-4, 3] = [-8, 1.5]. Path 2 now rotates: R [6, 2] = [-2, 6]. Different results, so SR is not RS.

blocks.caption: Multiply each by [3, 4] to reproduce the two paths.

blocks.md: Two properties do hold and you will use them constantly. Multiplication is **associative**: $A(BC) = (AB)C$. In words, multiplying $B$ by $C$ first and then applying $A$ gives the same matrix as multiplying $A$ by $B$ first and then applying that to $C$, because both describe one composition: apply $C$, then $B$, then $A$. So you may group a chain however is cheapest. And the **transpose** $A^\top$ (rows become columns, so entry $(i, j)$ moves to $(j, i)$) reverses order across a product: $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$, the transpose of $A$ times $B$ is $B$ transpose times $A$ transpose. Reason: entry $(i, j)$ of the left side is row $j$ of $A$ dotted with column $i$ of $B$, and that is row $i$ of $B^\top$ dotted with column $j$ of $A^\top$. A dot product is itself a tiny matrix product: treat a vector as an $n \times 1$ column, so its transpose is a $1 \times n$ row, and $\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}$, a $1 \times n$ times an $n \times 1$.

Cost grows fast. Two $4096 \times 4096$ matrices need $4096^3 \approx 6.87 \times 10^{10}$ multiply-adds, about $1.37 \times 10^{11}$ floating-point operations if you count the multiply and the add separately. This is why GPUs (graphics processing units, chips with thousands of arithmetic units working in parallel) are built around fast matrix multiplication and why ML performance discussions count FLOPs.

`A * B` in NumPy and PyTorch is the **element-wise** (Hadamard, after the mathematician Jacques Hadamard) product, which multiplies entries in matching positions, not matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is `A @ B` (or `np.matmul`). With two same-shape square matrices both run without error and give different answers, so this bug is silent.
$(m \times n)(n \times p) = (m \times p)$. Each entry is a row-column dot product, the product means apply the right matrix first, and order matters.

blocks.question: Q is $8 \times 64$ and K is $8 \times 64$. Which expression is a valid matrix product, and what is its shape?
options: Q @ K, shape 8 x 64
Q.T @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 8 x 8
blocks.explain: Inner sizes must match. $Q$ is $8\times64$ and $K^\top$ is $64\times8$, so $QK^\top$ is $8\times8$. $Q$ @ $K$ fails ($64 \ne 8$). $Q^\top K^\top$ would be $(64\times8)(64\times8)$, which also fails. This exact product returns in the last lesson, as attention scores.

blocks.question: You need $ABx$ where $A$ and $B$ are $1000 \times 1000$ and $x$ is a vector. Which order of evaluation is cheaper?
options: (AB)x, because multiplying matrices first is faster
A(Bx), because two matrix-vector products cost about 2 million multiply-adds versus about 1 billion for AB
They cost the same because multiplication is associative
Neither; you must invert A first
blocks.explain: Associativity guarantees the same answer, not the same cost. $AB$ alone is $1000^3 = 10^9$ multiply-adds. $B\mathbf{x}$ then $A(B\mathbf{x})$ is $2 \times 1000^2 = 2\times10^6$.

lessons.title: Span, independence and rank: what a matrix can reach

blocks.md: The column view says $A\mathbf{x}$ is a weighted sum of the columns of $A$. Turn that around and ask which outputs a matrix can produce at all. Tiny example: with $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$, can some input land on $[5, 0]$? Yes: $\mathbf{x} = [3, -1]$ gives $3[2,1] - 1[1,3] = [5, 0]$. With $B = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$ no input does, and this lesson explains why.

A **linear combination** of some vectors multiplies each by a number and adds the results, which is exactly what $A\mathbf{x}$ does with the columns. The **span** of a set of vectors is everything reachable this way, the set of all their linear combinations. So the outputs of $A\mathbf{x}$ are the span of the columns of $A$, called its **column space** (or range), and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ lies in it. $A$'s columns $[2,1]$ and $[1,3]$ do not lie on one line, and together they reach the whole plane.

Now look at $B$. Its second column $[2,4]$ is 2 times its first column $[1,2]$, so $B\mathbf{x} = x_1[1,2] + x_2[2,4] = (x_1 + 2x_2)[1,2]$. Every output is a multiple of $[1,2]$: $B$ squashes the whole plane onto one line through the origin, and the second column adds nothing to the span. Vectors like these are **linearly dependent**: one of them is a linear combination of the others. A set is **linearly independent** when none of them is, so each vector adds a new direction.

blocks.title: Five inputs sent through A and through B

scenes.caption: Five inputs, written as pairs. The first two are the basis vectors e1 and e2.
Under A, e1 and e2 land on its columns [2, 1] and [1, 3], and the outputs point in many directions, including [5, 0]. A's outputs fill the plane.
Under B every output is a multiple of [1, 2]: [1, 2], [2, 4] and [3, 6]. The whole plane collapses onto one line.
Worse, [1, 0] and [3, -1] both land on [1, 2], and [2, -1] lands on [0, 0]. Different inputs give the same output, so B loses information.

blocks.md: Now the basis claim from the matrix-vector lesson can be made precise. A **basis** of a space is a set of vectors that is linearly independent and whose span is the whole space. Then every vector is a combination of them in exactly one way: if two different combinations gave the same vector, subtracting them would give a combination equal to zero, and one vector could be written in terms of the others. $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2$ are a basis of the plane, and so are $A$'s columns.

The **rank** of a matrix is the dimension of its column space: how many independent directions its outputs can take, which equals the largest number of linearly independent columns. $A$ has rank 2; $B$ has rank 1, because its outputs fill only a line. Shape caps rank. A $3 \times 2$ matrix takes 2 numbers in, so its outputs are combinations of only 2 columns: at most a plane inside $\mathbb{R}^3$, and most targets in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are out of reach. In general an $m \times n$ matrix has rank at most the smaller of $m$ and $n$.

What does $B$ destroy? The inputs it sends to zero form its **null space**. Column by column, $B[2,-1] = 2[1,2] - 1[2,4] = [0,0]$, and every multiple of $[2,-1]$ also goes to zero. Adding a null-space vector to an input leaves the output unchanged: $[1,0] + [2,-1] = [3,-1]$, and both give $[1,2]$. So from $B\mathbf{x}$ alone you cannot tell which input you started with. A matrix keeps all information exactly when its null space holds only the zero vector, because a nonzero $\mathbf{x}$ with $B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is a combination of the columns that cancels, which is another way of saying the columns are dependent.

blocks.prompt: A $4 \times 4$ weight matrix has columns $\mathbf{c}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{c}_4$ with $\mathbf{c}_4 = \mathbf{c}_1 + \mathbf{c}_2$. What is its rank at most? Name one nonzero input it sends to zero.
blocks.reveal: **Rank at most 3**: $\mathbf{c}_4$ adds no direction that $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2$ do not already give. The input $[1, 1, 0, -1]$ gives $\mathbf{c}_1 + \mathbf{c}_2 - \mathbf{c}_4 = \mathbf{0}$, and so does every multiple of it. The layer therefore cannot tell $\mathbf{x}$ apart from $\mathbf{x} + t[1,1,0,-1]$ for any number $t$.

blocks.md: Rank is also a way to save parameters. Multiply a $d \times r$ matrix by an $r \times d$ matrix and the product is $d \times d$, but every output is the first matrix times an $r$-component vector, so it lies in the span of just $r$ columns: rank at most $r$. Storing the two factors costs $2dr$ numbers instead of $d^2$. **LoRA** (low-rank adaptation, Hu et al., 2021) fine-tunes large models this way: it freezes the pretrained weight $W_0$ and trains only an update $\Delta W = BA$, with $B$ of shape $d \times r$, $A$ of shape $r \times k$ and $r$ much smaller than $d$ and $k$ (the paper's letters, not this lesson's $A$ and $B$). For $d = k = 4096$ and $r = 8$ that is 65,536 trainable numbers instead of 16,777,216, 256 times fewer.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
B = np.array([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])       # column 2 = 2 x column 1
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A), np.linalg.matrix_rank(B))
print(B @ [1, 0], B @ [3, -1], B @ [2, -1])  # two inputs, one output

d, r = 4096, 8                           # LoRA-style update: (d x r) @ (r x d)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dW = rng.normal(size=(d, r)) @ rng.normal(size=(r, d))
print(dW.shape, np.linalg.matrix_rank(dW))
print(d * d, 2 * d * r)                  # numbers stored: full vs factored
# output:
# 2 1
# [1. 2.] [1. 2.] [0. 0.]
# (4096, 4096) 8
# 16777216 65536
blocks.caption: matrix_rank counts independent directions. A product of 4096 x 8 and 8 x 4096 random factors is a 4096 x 4096 matrix of rank 8.

blocks.md: Rank counts independent directions, not nonzero entries. $B$ has no zeros at all and rank 1, while the identity matrix is mostly zeros and has full rank. In floating point a matrix can also be *nearly* dependent, so `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank` counts singular values (from the SVD lesson) above a small tolerance.

The outputs of $A\mathbf{x}$ are the span of $A$'s columns. Columns that are combinations of others add nothing; the rank counts the independent directions that remain. Rank below the number of columns means a nonzero null space: different inputs collide and information is lost.

blocks.question: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$: $[1,0]$, $[0,1]$ and $[1,1]$. Which statement is right?
options: They are linearly independent, because no two of them are parallel
Their span is 3-dimensional, one dimension per vector
They are linearly dependent, and their span is the whole plane
They are dependent, so their span is only a line
blocks.explain: $[1,1] = [1,0] + [0,1]$, so the set is dependent, but the first two already reach every point of the plane. No two being parallel is not enough for independence. The plane has dimension 2, so no set of 3 vectors in it can be independent, and no span inside it can be 3-dimensional.

blocks.question: A layer has a $1024 \times 1024$ weight. You train only a low-rank update $\Delta W = BA$ with $B$ of shape $1024 \times 4$ and $A$ of shape $4 \times 1024$. How many trainable numbers, and what is the rank of $\Delta W$ at most?
options: 8,192 numbers, rank at most 4
1,048,576 numbers, rank at most 4
8,192 numbers, rank at most 1024
4,096 numbers, rank at most 8
blocks.explain: $B$ has $1024 \times 4$ and $A$ has $4 \times 1024$ entries: 8,192 in total. $\Delta W$ is $1024 \times 1024$, but every output passes through only 4 numbers ($A\mathbf{x}$), so its rank is at most 4. 1,048,576 is the full matrix you avoided training.

lessons.title: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b

blocks.md: The matrix-vector lesson computed $A\mathbf{x} = [4, 7]$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x} = [1, 2]$. The everyday problem runs the other way: you know the output $\mathbf{b} = [4, 7]$ and want the input. That is solving the **linear system** $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, here the two equations $2x_1 + x_2 = 4$ and $x_1 + 3x_2 = 7$. The last lesson showed how this fails: a matrix that squashes the plane onto a line cannot reach most outputs, and reaches the rest from many inputs. This lesson measures squashing with one number and builds the map that undoes $A$.

The **identity matrix** $I$ is the map that does nothing: 1s on the main diagonal (top left to bottom right) and 0s everywhere else, so $I\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}$ for every $\mathbf{x}$. Its columns are $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$: the axes stay where they are.

Now watch areas. The unit square, with corners $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$, has area 1. $A$ sends its sides $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ to the columns $[2,1]$ and $[1,3]$, so the square becomes the parallelogram with those two sides. Because $A$ is linear, every little square of the grid changes the same way, so all areas are multiplied by one common factor. That factor, with a sign attached, is the **determinant** $\det A$.

blocks.tex: \det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc, \qquad \det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 1 = 5
blocks.caption: Where it comes from (positive entries): the parallelogram with sides [a, c] and [b, d] sits in an (a + b) by (c + d) box. Removing two triangles of area ac/2, two of area bd/2 and two rectangles of area bc leaves ad - bc. For A: 12 - 2 - 3 - 2 = 5.

blocks.title: Where four matrices send the corners of the unit square

scenes.caption: The unit square, area 1. Each corner will be multiplied by a matrix; the images of (1, 0) and (0, 1) are the matrix's columns.
A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] moves the corners to (2, 1), (1, 3) and (3, 4): a parallelogram of area 5, so det A = 5.
B = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] sends every corner onto the line through [1, 2]. The square is flattened to zero area: det B = 1 x 4 - 2 x 2 = 0, matching its rank of 1.
The swap [[0, 1], [1, 0]] exchanges the axes. Area is kept but the square is turned over like a page: det = 0 x 0 - 1 x 1 = -1. A negative determinant means orientation is reversed.
Rotation by 90 degrees, [[0, -1], [1, 0]], turns the square without stretching or flipping it: det = 0 x 0 - (-1) x 1 = 1.

blocks.title: Area factor of [[2, 1], [1, c]] as c changes

scenes.caption: At c = 3 the matrix is A and areas grow 5 times.
At c = 1 the determinant is 2 - 1 = 1: shapes are skewed but areas are kept.
At c = 0.5 the columns [2, 1] and [1, 0.5] are parallel. The plane collapses onto a line and the determinant is 0.
At c = 0 the determinant is -1: the columns have passed through each other, so the map now flips orientation.

blocks.md: Two facts follow from the picture. A determinant of 0 means some direction is squashed flat, which is the same as rank below $n$ and a nonzero null space. And determinants multiply under composition, $\det(AB) = \det A \cdot \det B$: applying $B$ scales areas by $\det B$, then $A$ scales them by $\det A$. In 3 dimensions the determinant scales volumes, and in $n$ dimensions $n$-dimensional volume.

The **inverse** $A^{-1}$ is the matrix that undoes $A$: $A^{-1}A = I$. Then $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ gives $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix there is a closed form: swap the two diagonal entries, negate the other two, and divide by the determinant. For our $A$, $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$, and $A^{-1}[4,7] = \frac{1}{5}[12 - 7, -4 + 14] = [1, 2]$: the input is recovered.

blocks.caption: The formula divides by the determinant, so it breaks exactly when det A = 0.

blocks.md: So an inverse exists exactly when $\det A \ne 0$, which is the same as $A$ being square with independent columns (full rank). A square matrix with dependent columns, and so no inverse, is called **singular**. The picture explains why: once $B$ has flattened the plane, each output comes from many inputs, and no map can know which one to return. One more rule, by the same socks-and-shoes logic as the transpose: $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$. To undo apply $B$, then $A$, you first undo $A$, then $B$.

blocks.prompt: $R$ rotates the plane 90 degrees counterclockwise. Without using the formula, what is $R^{-1}$, and what is $\det R$?
blocks.reveal: $R^{-1}$ rotates 90 degrees **clockwise**: $\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$, which happens to be $R^\top$. And $\det R = 1$, because a rotation keeps every area and does not flip anything. The next lesson shows why the inverse of every rotation is its transpose.

blocks.md: In code, do not compute $A^{-1}$ to solve a system. Goodfellow et al. call the inverse mainly a theoretical tool: it is stored with limited precision, and algorithms that work with $\mathbf{b}$ directly usually get more accurate answers. `numpy.linalg.solve(A, b)` calls the routine `gesv` (general solve) from LAPACK (Linear Algebra PACKage, the standard library of dense linear algebra routines), which factors $A$ into triangular pieces (an LU factorization with partial pivoting), solves with those, and raises `LinAlgError` if $A$ is singular.

Nearly singular is the practical danger. $M = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1.0001\end{bmatrix}$ has almost parallel columns. Solving $M\mathbf{x} = [2, 2.0001]$ gives $[1, 1]$, but moving the second entry of $\mathbf{b}$ by 0.0001, to 2.0002, gives $[0, 2]$. The **condition number** measures this sensitivity: NumPy defines it as the norm of $M$ times the norm of $M^{-1}$, and it is about 40,002 here, versus 2.6 for $A$. Goodfellow et al. put it this way: when the condition number is large, matrix inversion is particularly sensitive to error in the input, so rounding errors in $\mathbf{b}$ become large errors in $\mathbf{x}$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([4., 7.])
print(np.linalg.det(A))           # area factor
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))      # x with A x = b, no inverse formed
print(np.linalg.inv(A) * 5)       # 5 A^-1 = [[3,-1],[-1,2]]

M = np.array([[1., 1.], [1., 1.0001]])   # nearly parallel columns
print(np.linalg.cond(M))
print(np.linalg.solve(M, [2., 2.0001]))
print(np.linalg.solve(M, [2., 2.0002]))  # b moved by 0.0001
# output:
# 5.000000000000001
# [1. 2.]
# [[ 3. -1.]
#  [-1.  2.]]
# 40002.00007491523
# [1. 1.]
# [0. 2.]
blocks.caption: solve finds x without forming the inverse; the last two lines show an ill-conditioned system amplifying a tiny change in b.

blocks.md: A tiny determinant does not by itself mean trouble. $0.1I$ in 10 dimensions has determinant $10^{-10}$ yet condition number 1: it shrinks every direction equally and is trivial to undo. Ill-conditioning is about *unequal* stretching, which the condition number (and the SVD lesson) measures.

$\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

blocks.question: For which matrix does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$?
blocks.explain: The determinants are $4 - 4 = 0$, $10 - 12 = -2$, $6 - 6 = 0$ and $0 - 0 = 0$. Only the second is nonzero, so only it is invertible. A negative determinant is fine: it means the map flips orientation, not that it loses information.

blocks.question: $\det A = 3$ and $\det B = -2$ for two $2 \times 2$ matrices. What is $\det(AB)$, and is $AB$ invertible?
options: -6, and AB is invertible
1, and AB is invertible
-6, and AB is not invertible because its determinant is negative
6, and AB is invertible
blocks.explain: Determinants multiply under composition: $3 \times (-2) = -6$. Any nonzero determinant means no direction is squashed flat, so $AB$ has an inverse, $B^{-1}A^{-1}$. The sign only records the orientation flip that $B$ introduces.

blocks.md: Four measurements: at $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$ you observe $y = 2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8$, and you want the slope $w$ in $y \approx wx$. That is four equations in one unknown ($1w = 2.1$, $2w = 3.9$, and so on), and no single $w$ satisfies all four. A tall system like this almost never has an exact solution, so the question becomes which $w$ comes closest. The answer is a projection, and projections are built from perpendicular vectors.

Two vectors are **orthogonal** when their dot product is 0, which the dot product lesson showed means perpendicular. A set of vectors is **orthonormal** when every pair is orthogonal and each has length 1. A square matrix whose columns are orthonormal is called an **orthogonal matrix** $Q$. Entry $(i, j)$ of $Q^\top Q$ is column $i$ dotted with column $j$: 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. So $Q^\top Q = I$, and the inverse is simply the transpose, $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$.

Example: $Q = \begin{bmatrix}0.6&-0.8\\0.8&0.6\end{bmatrix}$. Its columns have length $\sqrt{0.36+0.64} = 1$ and dot product $-0.48 + 0.48 = 0$. It rotates $[3,4]$ to $[-1.4, 4.8]$, still of length 5. That holds in general: $\|Q\mathbf{x}\|^2 = (Q\mathbf{x})^\top Q\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\top Q^\top Q\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}$, so an orthogonal matrix keeps every length, and by the same algebra every dot product and angle. Rotations are the familiar example, which is why the rotation $R$ in the last lesson had $R^{-1} = R^\top$.

The dot product lesson found how far $\mathbf{b}$ reaches along $\mathbf{a}$: the projection length $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}/\|\mathbf{a}\|$. To get the projection as a vector, walk that length along the unit vector $\mathbf{a}/\|\mathbf{a}\|$. With $\mathbf{a} = [3,4]$ and $\mathbf{b} = [1,2]$: $\mathbf{p} = \frac{11}{25}[3,4] = [1.32, 1.76]$, of length 2.2 as before. The leftover $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = [-0.32, 0.24]$ is the **residual**, and $\mathbf{e}\cdot\mathbf{a} = -0.96 + 0.96 = 0$: it is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$. That is what makes $\mathbf{p}$ the closest point on the line: any other point adds a step along $\mathbf{a}$ to that perpendicular error, and by Pythagoras the distance only grows.

blocks.caption: Projection of b onto the line through a. The residual b - p is orthogonal to a.

blocks.title: Squared distance from b = [1, 2] to the point t a on the line

x.label: t (the point is t times a = [3, 4])

scenes.caption: At t = 0 the candidate is the origin, at squared distance 1 + 4 = 5 from b.
At t = 0.2 the candidate [0.6, 0.8] is at squared distance 1.6. Moving along a helps.
At t = 0.44 = a.b / a.a the squared distance bottoms out at 0.16, the squared length of the residual [-0.32, 0.24]. This is the projection.
At t = 0.8 the candidate overshoots: squared distance 3.4. Only the projection makes the error perpendicular to a.

blocks.md: Least squares is the same idea with a column space in place of a line. Put the inputs as the columns of a tall matrix $X$, one row per measurement. Every weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ gives predictions $X\mathbf{w}$, a point in the column space of $X$. Closest means the smallest $\|\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}\|^2$, the sum of squared errors, hence the name **least squares**. The best $X\mathbf{w}$ is the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space, so the residual $\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}$ must be orthogonal to every column. Writing all those dot products at once gives $X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$, the **normal equations**.

blocks.caption: The normal equations. When the columns of X are independent, X^T X is invertible and there is exactly one best w.

blocks.md: With one column $X = [1,2,3,4]$: $X^\top X = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30$ and $X^\top\mathbf{y} = 2.1 + 7.8 + 18.6 + 31.2 = 59.7$, so $w = 59.7/30 = 1.99$. The residuals are $[0.11, -0.08, 0.23, -0.16]$, and their dot product with $[1,2,3,4]$ is $0.11 - 0.16 + 0.69 - 0.64 = 0$, as promised. Add a column of ones for an intercept $c$ in $y \approx wx + c$ and the normal equations become $2 \times 2$, with $X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix}30&10\\10&4\end{bmatrix}$, $X^\top\mathbf{y} = [59.7, 20]$ and solution $w = 1.94$, $c = 0.15$. The sum of squared errors drops from 0.097 to 0.082: an extra column can only enlarge the column space and bring the projection closer.

blocks.title: Least-squares lines through four points

scenes.caption: One column: the best line through the origin has slope 1.99. Squared errors sum to 0.097.
Adding the intercept column lets the line shift up by 0.15 and tilt to 1.94; the squared errors fall to 0.082. Both residual vectors are orthogonal to their columns.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
y = np.array([2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8])
X = np.column_stack([x, np.ones(4)])      # columns: x and an intercept of ones
w = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)     # normal equations
print(w)
r = y - X @ w                             # residual
print(np.round(r, 2), np.allclose(X.T @ r, 0))  # orthogonal to both columns
print(np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0])   # library route, same answer
# output:
# [1.94 0.15]
# [ 0.01 -0.13  0.23 -0.11] True
# [1.94 0.15]
blocks.caption: The normal equations and numpy.linalg.lstsq agree. The residual is orthogonal to both columns.

blocks.md: Orthonormal bases are so convenient that there is a standard recipe for building one, **Gram-Schmidt** orthogonalization (after the mathematicians Jorgen Pedersen Gram and Erhard Schmidt): keep the first vector, scaled to length 1; from each next vector subtract its projections onto the ones already kept, then scale what is left to length 1. From $[3,4]$ and $[1,2]$: $\mathbf{q}_1 = [0.6, 0.8]$; $[1,2]$ minus its projection $2.2\,\mathbf{q}_1 = [1.32, 1.76]$ leaves $[-0.32, 0.24]$, of length 0.4, so $\mathbf{q}_2 = [-0.8, 0.6]$. These are exactly the columns of the rotation $Q$ above.

The normal equations are the clearest derivation but not the best code. The condition number of $X^\top X$ is the square of that of $X$ (the SVD lesson shows why), so a mildly ill-conditioned $X$ becomes a badly conditioned system. Call `numpy.linalg.lstsq(X, y)`, which takes $X$ itself. Its answer equals $X^+\mathbf{y}$, where $X^+$ is the **Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse**, the stand-in for an inverse when $X$ is not square.

Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles, and $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$. Projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto a line or a column space leaves a residual orthogonal to it, and that orthogonality condition, $X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$, is least squares.

blocks.question: After a least-squares fit, the residual is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}$. Which statement must hold?
options: r is the zero vector
r points in the same direction as y
r is orthogonal to every column of X
r has the same length as y
blocks.explain: The best fit is the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space, so the leftover is perpendicular to that space: $X^\top\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$. It is zero only if $\mathbf{y}$ was already reachable, which a tall noisy system almost never is.

blocks.question: Project $\mathbf{b} = [2, 1]$ onto the line through $\mathbf{a} = [1, 1]$. What is $\mathbf{p}$?
blocks.explain: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 3$ and $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a} = 2$, so $\mathbf{p} = 1.5[1,1]$. Check: $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p} = [0.5, -0.5]$, whose dot product with $[1,1]$ is 0. $[3,3]$ forgets to divide by $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}$, which you may skip only when $\mathbf{a}$ has length 1.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches

blocks.md: Apply $S = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ to three vectors. $[1,0]$ goes to $[2,1]$: it turns. $[1,1]$ goes to $[3,3]$: same direction, 3 times longer. $[1,-1]$ goes to $[2-1, 1-2] = [1,-1]$: unchanged. Most vectors are knocked off their line, but a few special directions are only stretched. Those directions explain what happens when a matrix is applied again and again, which networks and training algorithms do all the time.

An **eigenvector** of a square matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ that $A$ only scales: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$. The scale factor $\lambda$ (the Greek letter lambda) is its **eigenvalue**. Eigen is a German word meaning characteristic, self or own: these are the matrix's own directions. Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also one, with the same eigenvalue, so what matters is the line. For $S$, $[1,1]$ has eigenvalue 3 and $[1,-1]$ has eigenvalue 1. A negative eigenvalue flips vectors along their line; an eigenvalue of 0 means the direction is squashed to zero, so it lies in the null space.

How do you find them? $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ is the same as $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v}$ nonzero, so $A - \lambda I$ must squash a direction to zero: by the determinant lesson, $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. For $S$ that is $(2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = 0$, so $\lambda = 3$ or $\lambda = 1$. For the 90 degree rotation it is $\lambda^2 + 1 = 0$, which has no real solution: a rotation turns every vector off its own line, so it has no real eigenvectors. A shear $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ has just one eigenvector line, the first axis.

Eigenvectors turn repeated multiplication into simple powers. Write $[1,0]$ in eigenvector pieces, $[1,0] = 0.5[1,1] + 0.5[1,-1]$. Each application of $S$ multiplies each piece by its own eigenvalue, so after $k$ steps $S^k[1,0] = 0.5 \cdot 3^k[1,1] + 0.5[1,-1]$. The first piece grows like $3^k$ while the second stays put, so the direction swings toward $[1,1]$, which points at 45 degrees.

blocks.title: Applying S = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] to [1, 0] again and again

scenes.caption: k = 0: the start [1, 0], at 0 degrees.
k = 2: [5, 4] = 4.5[1, 1] + 0.5[1, -1]. The [1, 1] piece grew 3 times, the other did not.
k = 5: [122, 121] = 121.5[1, 1] + 0.5[1, -1], 44.8 degrees. The direction has locked onto the top eigenvector while the length explodes like 3^k.

blocks.md: This is **power iteration**: multiply by the matrix, rescale to length 1, repeat. It converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue is largest in absolute value, provided the start has some component along it; the MML book recommends it when only the top eigenvector is needed. The unwanted piece shrinks relative to the wanted one by the ratio of the eigenvalues, here 1/3 per step. The same arithmetic explains exploding and vanishing values in recurrent networks (networks that apply the same weight matrix at every step of a sequence) (Goodfellow et al., section 10.7): repeated multiplication by one matrix grows along eigenvalues above 1 in absolute value and decays along those below 1.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
S = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 2.]])
x = np.array([1., 0.])
for k in range(6):
    x = S @ x
    x = x / np.linalg.norm(x)            # keep only the direction
print(np.round(x, 4))                    # close to [1, 1]/sqrt(2)
print(np.round(x @ S @ x, 4))            # stretch along x: close to 3
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)           # for symmetric matrices
print(vals)
print(np.round(vecs, 4))
# output:
# [0.7081 0.7061]
# 3.0
# [1. 3.]
# [[-0.7071  0.7071]
#  [ 0.7071  0.7071]]
blocks.caption: Six steps of power iteration on S, then numpy.linalg.eigh, which returns eigenvalues in ascending order and unit eigenvectors as columns (their signs are arbitrary).

blocks.prompt: Start power iteration on $S$ from $[1,-1]$ instead of $[1,0]$. Where does it end up?
blocks.reveal: **It never moves.** $[1,-1]$ is itself an eigenvector, with eigenvalue 1, and it has no component along $[1,1]$ for the factor 3 to amplify, so every step returns $[1,-1]$ exactly. This is why power iteration starts from a random vector: a random start has some component along the top eigenvector.

blocks.md: Symmetric matrices, equal to their own transpose like $S$, are the well-behaved case and the one ML meets most: Hessians (matrices of curvatures, used below), covariance matrices (which record how pairs of features vary together) and $X^\top X$ are all symmetric. The **spectral theorem** (spectrum is the name for a matrix's set of eigenvalues, hence also spectral norm later) says a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Put those eigenvectors as the columns of an orthogonal $Q$ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\Lambda$ (capital lambda), and $S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$: rotate into the eigenvector axes, stretch each axis by its eigenvalue, rotate back.

blocks.caption: Q holds the unit eigenvectors [1, 1]/sqrt(2) and [1, -1]/sqrt(2). Also det S = 3 x 1 = 3 and the trace (sum of the diagonal) 2 + 2 = 3 + 1: for any square matrix the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues and the trace their sum, counting complex eigenvalues and repeats.

blocks.md: A preview of where this returns in training. **Gradient descent** fits a model by repeatedly nudging its numbers downhill on the loss (the number that scores how wrong the model is), with step size set by the **learning rate** $\eta$. Near a minimum the loss is shaped like a bowl, and the **Hessian** $H$, a symmetric matrix of curvatures saying how sharply the bowl bends in each direction, describes it. On such a quadratic bowl one step multiplies the error vector by $I - \eta H$. If $H\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $(I - \eta H)\mathbf{v} = (1 - \eta\lambda)\mathbf{v}$: same eigenvectors, eigenvalues $1 - \eta\lambda$. With $H = S$ and $\eta = 0.6$ the factors are $1 - 1.8 = -0.8$ and $0.4$, so both directions shrink. At $\eta = 0.7$ the factor along $[1,1]$ is $-1.1$: the error flips sign and grows every step. Stability needs $\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}$, here $2/3$. A symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues are all positive is called **positive definite**: for a Hessian that means a true bowl, curving up in every direction.

blocks.title: Per-step error factor 1 - eta lambda along each eigenvector

scenes.caption: H = S has eigenvalues 3 and 1. The sharp direction's factor crosses -1 at eta = 2/3; beyond that its error grows.
Make the sharp curvature 4 and the limit drops to 0.5, while the flat direction (eigenvalue 1) still shrinks by only 1 - eta per step. The largest eigenvalue sets the step size for every direction.

blocks.md: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$: eigenvectors are the directions $A$ only stretches, eigenvalues the stretch factors, found from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. Repeated multiplication is dominated by the largest $|\lambda|$. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors: $S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$.

blocks.question: A $2 \times 2$ matrix has eigenvalues 0.5 and 1.2 with independent eigenvectors. You apply it 50 times to a random vector. What happens?
options: The vector shrinks toward 0 because one eigenvalue is below 1
The vector stays about the same length, because 0.5 x 1.2 is close to 1
The vector grows and turns toward the eigenvector with eigenvalue 1.2
The vector turns toward the eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.5
blocks.explain: The two components are scaled by $1.2^{50} \approx 9100$ and $0.5^{50} \approx 9 \times 10^{-16}$. The first dominates, so the vector grows and aligns with that eigenvector. The product of the eigenvalues (the determinant) tracks areas, not the length of one vector.

blocks.question: A quadratic loss has a Hessian with eigenvalues 8 and 0.5. Which of these learning rates is the largest that still converges along every direction?
blocks.explain: Stability needs $\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 2/8 = 0.25$, so 0.24 works (factor $1 - 8 \times 0.24 = -0.92$). 4 is $2/0.5$, the limit for the flat direction only, and 1 also diverges along the sharp one. 0.125 converges but is not the largest.

lessons.title: The SVD: rotate, stretch, rotate, then keep what matters

blocks.md: Eigenvectors need a square matrix and are only guaranteed perpendicular when it is symmetric. Take the non-symmetric $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&0\\4&5\end{bmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 5 (from $\det(A - \lambda I) = (3-\lambda)(5-\lambda)$), yet it stretches some vectors by more than 5: the unit vector $[1,1]/\sqrt2$ goes to $[3,9]/\sqrt2$, of length 6.708. The **singular value decomposition** (SVD) describes the stretching correctly, and Goodfellow et al. note that every real matrix has one, square or not.

blocks.caption: U and V are orthogonal; Sigma (capital sigma) is diagonal, holding the singular values sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= ... >= 0. Read right to left: rotate (V^T), stretch each axis (Sigma), rotate (U).

blocks.md: Read the factors right to left, as with any product. $V^\top$ is orthogonal, so it only rotates (or reflects) the input, lining up special input directions $\mathbf{v}_i$, the **right singular vectors**, with the axes. $\Sigma$ stretches axis $i$ by the **singular value** $\sigma_i$. $U$ rotates the result onto output directions $\mathbf{u}_i$, the **left singular vectors**. So $A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$: perpendicular input directions go to perpendicular output directions, stretched. The circle of unit vectors becomes an ellipse whose semi-axes are $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ long.

How to find them: $A^\top A = V\Sigma^\top U^\top U\Sigma V^\top = V\Sigma^2V^\top$ is symmetric, so the $\mathbf{v}_i$ are its eigenvectors and the $\sigma_i$ the square roots of its eigenvalues. Here $A^\top A = \begin{bmatrix}25&20\\20&25\end{bmatrix}$, with eigenvectors $[1,1]$ and $[1,-1]$ and eigenvalues 45 and 5. So $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{45} \approx 6.708$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt5 \approx 2.236$, and $\mathbf{u}_i = A\mathbf{v}_i/\sigma_i$ gives $\mathbf{u}_1 = [1,3]/\sqrt{10}$ and $\mathbf{u}_2 = [3,-1]/\sqrt{10}$. Check: $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = \det A$.

blocks.title: A v1 in three moves: rotate, stretch, rotate

scenes.caption: Start with v1 = [1, 1]/sqrt(2), a unit vector.
V^T turns v1 onto the first axis: [1, 0]. With v2 = [1, -1]/sqrt(2), V (and U below) is a reflection, the "or reflects" case; like a rotation it keeps the length at 1.
Sigma stretches axis 1 by sigma_1 = 6.708 (axis 2 would be stretched by 2.236).
U (a reflection here, like V) turns the result onto u1 = [1, 3]/sqrt(10): [2.121, 6.364], exactly A v1 = [3, 9]/sqrt(2).
The same three moves send v2 = [1, -1]/sqrt(2) to [2.121, -0.707], of length 2.236 = sigma_2. Its dot product with A v1 is 4.5 - 4.5 = 0: the ellipse's axes are perpendicular.

blocks.md: Singular values are not eigenvalues in general: $A$ has eigenvalues 5 and 3 but singular values 6.708 and 2.236. They agree for symmetric matrices with nonnegative eigenvalues; for $S$ from the last lesson both are 3 and 1. The largest singular value is the most any unit vector can be stretched, the **spectral norm** $\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1$, which bounds how much a layer can amplify its input. The ratio $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ is the condition number from the determinant lesson: 3 for this $A$. Since $A^\top A = V\Sigma^2V^\top$, its singular values are the $\sigma_i^2$ and its condition number is the square, 9 here: the reason the least-squares lesson warns against forming $X^\top X$. And the rank is the number of nonzero singular values, which is how `matrix_rank` counts it.

The sum form $A = \sum_i \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^\top$ writes any matrix as a stack of rank-1 pieces (each $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\top$ is a column times a row, so all its columns are multiples of $\mathbf{u}$), ordered from most to least important. Keeping the first $r$ pieces gives a rank-$r$ matrix, and the **Eckart-Young theorem** says no rank-$r$ matrix is closer (the mathematicians Carl Eckart and Gale Young proved it in 1936 for the Frobenius norm; Leon Mirsky extended it to the spectral norm in 1960). In the spectral norm the error is exactly $\sigma_{r+1}$, the first singular value you dropped.

Example: 6 users rate 4 items (made-up data). Users 1 to 3 like items 1 and 2, users 4 and 5 like items 3 and 4, and user 6 rates everything 3. The singular values are 13.32, 8.63, 1.58 and 1.22: two large and two small, because the table is mostly two tastes. Keeping two pieces reproduces every rating within 0.53, the Frobenius error is 12.5 percent of the table's own Frobenius norm, and the spectral error is 1.58, exactly $\sigma_3$. A rank-$r$ approximation of an $m \times n$ matrix stores $r(m+n)$ numbers (fold each $\sigma_i$ into $\mathbf{u}_i$): 20 instead of 24 here, a small saving, but 65,536 instead of 16.8 million for a $4096 \times 4096$ matrix at $r = 8$.

blocks.title: A 6 x 4 ratings table and its low-rank approximations

scenes.caption: The original ratings. Two blocks of taste plus one user who likes everything equally.
Rank 1, sigma_1 u1 v1^T: one average taste. Every user gets roughly the same pattern, scaled. Spectral error 8.63 = sigma_2.
Rank 2 (shown rounded): both tastes are back and every entry is within 0.53 of the original. Spectral error 1.58 = sigma_3, the best any rank-2 matrix can do.
Back to the original for comparison: what rank 2 dropped is the small noise inside each block.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[3., 0.], [4., 5.]])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
print(s)                                  # singular values
print(np.allclose(U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt, A))
print(np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)          # eigenvalues differ

R = np.array([[5, 4, 1, 1], [4, 5, 1, 0], [5, 5, 0, 1],
              [1, 0, 5, 4], [0, 1, 4, 5], [3, 3, 3, 3]], float)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(R, full_matrices=False)
print(np.round(s, 3))
R2 = U[:, :2] * s[:2] @ Vt[:2]            # keep the top 2 pieces
print(round(np.linalg.norm(R - R2, 2), 3))  # spectral error = s[2]
print(round(np.linalg.norm(R - R2) / np.linalg.norm(R), 3))
# output:
# [6.70820393 2.23606798]
# True
# [5. 3.]
# [13.321  8.635  1.58   1.224]
# 1.58
# 0.125
blocks.caption: The 2 x 2 example and the ratings table. The spectral error of the rank-2 approximation equals the third singular value, as Eckart-Young says.

blocks.md: **Principal component analysis** (PCA) is the SVD applied to data. Put $N$ data points as the rows of a matrix, subtract the mean point from every row (**centering**), and take the SVD. The first right singular vector $\mathbf{v}_1$ is the direction along which the points spread the most, the share of the spread (the variance) along $\mathbf{v}_i$ is $\sigma_i^2/\sum_j\sigma_j^2$, and projecting each centered point onto $\mathbf{v}_1$, one dot product, compresses it to a single number with the least possible squared reconstruction error. Goodfellow et al. derive PCA in exactly these terms, as the best linear compression onto orthonormal directions.

Example: the six points $(1,2), (2,3), (3,3), (4,5), (5,5), (6,6)$ have mean $(3.5, 4)$. After centering, the SVD gives $\mathbf{v}_1 = [0.772, 0.635]$, about 39 degrees up from the first axis, carrying 98.4 percent of the variance. Each point becomes one number, its dot product with $\mathbf{v}_1$: $-3.201, -1.794, -1.021, 1.021, 1.794, 3.201$. Mapping those back onto the line puts every point within 0.46 of where it started.

curves.label: first component v1 through the mean

scenes.caption: The first principal direction passes through the mean along v1 = [0.772, 0.635]. The points hug it: 98.4 percent of the variance lies along this line.
show: first component v1 through the mean

scenes.caption: The second direction v2 = [0.635, -0.772] is perpendicular and carries the remaining 1.6 percent. Dropping it is the 1D compression.
